utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. It's case IT-04-74-T, Prosecutor versus Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused. Ladies and gentlemen, before we continue our work, I would like, on behalf of the Chamber, to thank the registrar, who is going to leave us to occupy another position in the Registry, and I want to express to him all our gratitude for all the work he has done in this case and wish him luck in his next job. And the Trial Chamber wishes to note that he has extremely successfully and diligently performed his job in our courtroom. With greatest affection and the best wishes, we will say good-bye to him. Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence bar, associate us with what you said about Mr. Sabbah. He has indeed, with great, good humour put up with this collection of Defence lawyers and what a wonderful job. And we also extend our very best wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on behalf of the Prosecution, Mr. Sabbah has been, as everyone has noted, a very valuable and extremely helpful member of the courtroom. We thank him for his service and wish him the best.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was an honour and pleasure to work with all of you and I wish all of you the very best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we please move into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning time, I think Mr. Ibrisimovic will use between three-quarters and an hour, and the Prlic Defence will use the 45 minutes. They were approved. I don't know who will start. The Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I think I will use most of my time, and if some time is left, Mr. Coric asked for approval to ask some questions himself. Concerning the problem yesterday with the 13 bundles of documentation, we prepared copies today and created another bundle that unites all the documents that the Prosecution used yesterday. I would like both bundles to be given the witness if that's possible. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I have many questions for you, but I will ask them in a way that will allow you to answer with a yes, no, I don't know, or I don't remember, so that we can go through all of them. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In his examination-in-chief, the Prosecution showed you a variety of documents containing references to Berislav Pusic. Sometimes that name was written in hand. When you were shown those documents you said Berislav Pusic enjoyed authority, in your eyes, as an officer of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see in e-court P 01773. And for the Chamber, it's in bundle 1. I would like to move immediately to page 2. It's a document of the military police crime prevention service from the -- from April 1993. The subject is the staffing organisation, and it says: "Berislav Pusic and Goran Milicevic who have so far worked in this department are hereby taken off the list. Milicevic is hereby nominated for commander of the Military Police Platoon in Siroki Brijeg, and Berislav Pusic is nominated to become an officer of control at the administration of the military police or officer for cooperation and liaison with the opposite side in connection with exchange of prisoners." We see that they were taken off the list of employees of the military police on the 1st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic, you are speaking too fast for interpretation. Do try to speak a little more slowly. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see there a mistake in the transcript. I said they were taken off the list of the crime prevention service in the military police, not the military police itself. Tell me, sir, did you ever see this appointment of Berislav Pusic to the position of control officer or liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are you aware with the regulations of the military police that govern the organisation and structure of the military police, its purview, and the staffing arrangements within the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I best know is the prison system, and later I learned about the system beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say later, when later?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As one of the officials of the military police, I later became familiar with the system of military police and continued to be there until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any documents about the system and the structure, and which documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I only knew about the structure of the prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you also have to speak a little more slowly, because you are giving interpreters a very hard time. Yes, proceed, and please try to -- not to overlap with counsel. Leave a brief pause between questions and answers. Yes, proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that in 1992 you were only familiar with the document governing the system of the prison, it's a document we've seen before on several occasions. It was also called house rules. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions on work that describes the staffing structure, the tasks and assignments of every employee in what you call house rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now see in e-court -- no, in fact I have another question. Do you know the description of the control officer's job? What does that imply?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see in e-court P 03191. That is also in the first bundle. It's a decision appointing Mr. Berislav Pusic head of service for the exchange of detained and other persons, dated 5th July, 1993. Tell me, do you know that Berislav Pusic was in this position as of the 5th of July as written here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the decision for the first time. And as for the fact, I mentioned it, that it was in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now like to move on to another subject. Tell me, in your examination-in-chief you said that after the establishment of the 5th Battalion of the military police, which according to you happened in June 1993, work in prison continued as before, but from that time on you leaned for logistics on the 5th Battalion. When you say "logistics," does that mean that you procured coupons for fuel from the 5th Battalion, equipment and badges for the security detail, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now see in e-court, see a document from the second bundle, P 02285. That's a document that was also shown to you before by the Prosecution. It's an order for release from Heliodrom dated 11th May, which specifies that the persons -- or person named is released after Mr. Berislav Pusic and Valentin Coric interceded.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were shown this document, you said that Valentin Coric would be named in that -- in such a document only very rarely. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to come back to the 9th of May, 1993, to clarify certain things with you. We've all read your diary, and we found some interesting points there that were not mentioned during the examination-in-chief. So tell me, is it true that when a large group of people arrived at Heliodrom on that day, on the 9th of May, 1993, you were informed that those people had, for their own safety and security, been displaced from the combat zone, and also that those people left Heliodrom within several days. That's written in your diary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little question from me. The document that we see now before us concerning the release of Muhiba Jugo, it says it was done at the intervention of Mr. Berko Pusic and Mr. Valentin Coric. So on the 5th of July, 1993, he was head of service for exchange of prisoners. So prior to his appointment to that post, what position did Mr. Pusic occupy? In what capacity exactly did he intercede for somebody to be released, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon the departure of the chief of the criminal prevention service of the military police, Dragan Barbaric was his name, I learnt that in his place Berislav Pusic arrived, and that was when he was in this post within the administration of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to go back to the 5th of May now -- 9th of May, sorry. But before I do so, you told me earlier on that you didn't see the appointment papers of Mr. Berislav Pusic to occupy the post for control or as a person in charge of exchange after the document dated the 1st of April, which I showed you, from the crime prevention department of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't that intimate, nor did I have an opportunity to see the document, and the man wouldn't have shown it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now to go back to the 9th of May. A large group of people arrived. We've already said that. And we've said that you were told that they had been transferred because of the war situation. We also said that they were released within a few days. Tell me now, please, when these people arrived, their registration and their accommodation and taking in was dealt with -- by Ms. Biljana Nikic, and Mr. Marko Bevanda from the office for displaced persons and refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have on e-court now the following document -- now, if it isn't on e-court, we have an example for the ELMO. It's in bundle 2. It is 5D 2016, 5D 02016. And you can find it in your bundle, sir. It's the first document in the second bundle. 5D -- it's the first document. It's a document from the office for displaced persons and refugees, and it is a list of individuals who are leaving Heliodrom. The list contains the names of 578 persons, and the date refers to the period from the 14th of May, 1993, to the 18th of May, 1993. The signature is that of Mr. Darinko Tadic. Tell us, please, do you know that Mr. Darinko Tadic was the head of the office for displaced persons and refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, but I forgot his first name. I hadn't forgotten his surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this document we can see that this same office, the office for displaced persons and refugees, in the period between the 14th to the 18th of May, 1993, registered 578 persons who left Heliodrom. Now, are these people that we said had arrived at Heliodrom on the 9th of May, in your opinion? Are those the same people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in view of everything we've said so far linked to these people, and in view of the office dealing with these people, I conclude that these people at Heliodrom had a sort of refugee status. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to questions from my learned friend Nozica linked to the food of the detainees, you said that it was all prepared, the meals were prepared in the central kitchen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an important document that is being presented here by the Defence and which requires a precision that the Judges would like to have. This document establishes that 578 individuals were leaving Heliodrom on the 18th of May, 1993, and it was signed by the person responsible of the head of the office for refugees and displaced persons. So we have this list of 578 persons, but there's a little uncertitude with a number 576, because there's a question mark by that name. But if we consider that these 578 people were refugees, as considered by the office in question, what I would like to know, sir, is this: When on the 9th of May these persons arrived at Heliodrom, I would like you to be more specific and tell me what conditions, how were they accommodated and taken in? Were they admitted by the responsible persons from that office, and you gave us two names? And when they arrived, how were they received by these people, and were these people registered as having arrived at Heliodrom? So to the best of your recollections, do you know this or not? If not, say you don't and we'll move on, but if you can help us out on this point and tell us to the best of your recollection how all this evolved, this could be useful to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th of May, when the people started arriving, the women and children and men, when they started arriving at Heliodrom -- or, rather, when they came to the building next door to the prison, they were put up -- or, rather, Marko Bevanda and Biljana Nikic dealt with them. She, Biljana, received the people and registered their names. They were accommodated in the prison building. In the prison building, at the time, there was just one department for prisoners -- or, rather, there was just one room where prisoners were serving their sentence, and they were physically separated from the people who were arriving. The prison itself, the prison building, as a prison, was a place where there were guards and a place where there was security details working that day doing their normal shifts. They were on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question. These two people that you mentioned, Bevanda and Biljana Nikic, received these people, took their names and so on, and you explained to us that they were put up in the prison, but apparently you separated -- they were separated from the prisoners, and you make that distinction. Now, if one of the 578 people brought in said, "I wish to call my aunt," for example, "who is in Rome. I want to phone her up," or, "I want to go out to buy an apple," or things like that, what would have happened? A schoolroom example. Would you have prevented them from doing that or what? What would you personally have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Faced with a situation like that, as care of these people was taken over by Mr. Marko Bevanda and Biljana Nikic, this request would have been forwarded to Marko and Biljana, and what the person, the lady, would have asked me, she would have ask them, had to ask them, and it was up to them whether they gave permission for that or not. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An additional question as a follow-up: They were put in the prison building because in the prison building the prison had the best conditions, living conditions, at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to the question of the central kitchen. You said that the meals and food for the detainees was prepared in this central kitchen. Now, the central kitchen was a kitchen belonging to the 3rd Brigade located at Heliodrom, and via the 3rd Brigade and their kitchen, the meals for the prisoners was organised. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true and correct that you had the same food, that the employees of the prison had the same food as the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have on e-court the following document: 502533. It's in the first bundle. 502533, the first bundle. In the Croatian version. I would like to look at page 1, line 9 and in the English version it is on page 2. P 02533 is the document number. It's also a document from the office for displaced persons and refugees, and I'm going to read out the paragraph that I'm interested in, where it says the following: "Together with other organisations and institutions, we took in and had under our care about 150.000 refugees and displaced persons." We have the wrong document. 2533 is the number. On e-court we have 5233. We need document 2533 on e-court, please. I'll read on: "We provided sufficient quantities of humanitarian aid of all kinds, several thousand tonnes, and thanks to that, we succeeded in ensuring normal living conditions for about 2.000 individuals at Heliodrom without assistance from other organisations." Tell me, please, do you know about this, and is what it says here correct, that the office for displaced persons and refugees procured humanitarian aid and assistance to cater to the individuals at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir -- and now I'd like to go back to the releases. Is it correct that in 1993, especially after May onwards, different -- all sorts of different people came in to bring in orders and intervene to have people released from the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show you a number of documents now to take a brief look at them, and then I'll go ahead and ask you my questions. On e-court -- or, rather, it is from bundle 6, Prosecution bundle 6, and we'll see it on e-court. So look at your screen, please, sir. 502439 is the number of the first document. 502439, not 5, P, P 0, Prosecution 02439. It is an order by the anti-terrorist group named Baja Kraljevic dated the 18th of May, 1993. The signature is illegible, but the person issues an order that a person incarcerated in Heliodrom be released immediately. It's a short document. Let's look at the next document which is P 02325, and it is also to be found in bundle 6. While we're waiting for that, I'll explain what the document is about. It's an order from Mr. Stanko Bozic dated the 12th of May, 1993, in which it says the following: "That pursuant to orders from Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, the following persons," and five are listed, "are to be released immediately." We can go on to the third document now. It is P 02443. And it is an order from Ivica Pusic, the commander of the brigade SIS, of the 3rd Brigade dated the 18th of May, 1993, and he too is calling for the release of a certain person after an interview has been conducted. Now, we have seen these three documents and we have seen that they are all orders from Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and the chief of the brigade SIS as well as the commander of the ATG, Baja Kraljevic, an officer there. Now, looking at these three documents I assume that you received orders from various people and you had to comply with them; you couldn't refuse. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These orders --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give me a yes or no answer, please. Could you refuse to comply or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer my question first and then go on to explain. Could you say, "Mr. Tuta, I'm not going to release those people"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the people that you mentioned here, I don't think this name of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and Ivica Pusic, that these are rare examples. And of the many releases, you name Zeljko Starac, for example. He never ever wrote again and never asked anybody to be released again. So this was a very rare occasion. Most of these were signed by Mr. Berko Pusic and the staff of the crime prevention service working in the military police. That's where they -- the orders came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Their Honours have the bundles. They'll be able to see whose orders they were, but I'm asking you a very simple question. When these people sent in their order for release, did you have to comply or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same request was sent to Mr. Marko Bevanda and Biljana Nikic, and they gave the response. They said whether they could be released or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about you. If you don't want to answer, that's fine, we'll move on, but I'm asking you about Tuta and these other people, whether you could have refused them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to say that. So, madam counsel, I want to tell the truth. You want to interpret it in your own way. So, Your Honours, may I be brief but to be clear as well?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you are neither brief nor being very clear and I would like to move on because I don't have enough time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that we have before us introduces an element of confusion because we have a document dated the 18th of May which is signed by Ivica Pusic from the SIS which requests the release of Badzak, who is in prison. Now, apparently this man Badzak was not a refugee. He was in prison. Because a refugee by definition is not a prisoner, whereas here, apparently, the author of this document considers Badzak to be in prison. Now, you probably don't remember the circumstances surrounding Badzak, but if Badzak was indeed a prisoner, which means he was separated from the other detainees, and if this Badzak was a refugee, then the document should have been addressed to the office for displaced persons and refugees, not addressed to the commander or the warden of the prison. Do you have an explanation for that -- to give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is addressed to refugees who were located and put up in prison as displaced persons, everything that needed to be done was forwarded to Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda, and they decided about whether these people were released and not the prison staff, not me. Now, if this was a question of a prisoner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree there, but -- yes, you're quite right from the point of view of the law and the regulations. It was up to the office to regulate that. But apparently we have a document which says that Badzak is a prisoner. Now, is that a mistake on the part of the person addressing this order, or do you have another explanation? I don't know. We're trying to see through this as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In reading the document, Badzak seems to have been in detention. Now, Mr. Ivica Pusic was the assistant commander of the 3rd Brigade for security, and he had the right to release a person whom he had interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In reading this, and I'm going to be brief, I don't want to take up Defence time. If we look at the first paragraph it says: "Please release ... Badzak, residing in Mostar, number 17 Husinske Bune street." Which might lead one to conclude that he left on the 9th of May -- this is his supposition, that he left his house on the 9th of May and that he was in Heliodrom as a refugee. But in the second paragraph, he goes on to explain. He had a preliminary interview conducted by somebody at SIS. After the 9th of May and following that interview, we get this request for the release of this person. Now, to the best of your knowledge, these refugees in inverted commas, alleged refugees, were there members of SIS that came to the prison to conduct interviews and have meetings with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially if it refers to this case. Mr. Ivica Pusic was also placed within the perimeter of Heliodrom, and he probably brought it himself. And based on this paper he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. Perhaps the witness should be advised of his rights again, that he's here to tell the whole truth, not part of the truth. He should answer the questions. And he's here to answer the questions truthfully and completely. He's not doing that. He's obfuscating. He's obviously giving my colleague a hard time. He's not answering the questions. He must be warned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, so far I had the impression that you understood what you were being told. Counsel is asking you a precise question and I'm asking you a precise question, neither of which you're answering. My question was: Did SIS investigators come to meet the "refugees" between the 9th and the 18th of May? That's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see SIS people at all while the refugees were at the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, Counsel, proceed and the Chamber will try to assist you in getting exactly the answers to your question. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I didn't get an answer to my previous question concerning the order, but I will move on. We have the entire documentation. Can we see P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I might also try to be of some assistance. It seems to me -- but, Witness, you please verify and confirm what I say. I thought that your answer to the question of counsel, whether you had to obey to anyone who ordered or wanted you to order a release, your answer was it was not you to decide, but this went directly to Biljana and the other gentleman, and they took the decision. You did not take a decision at all. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it didn't concern refugees, if it concerned prisoners, because you said the two categories were separated, who decided then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About prisoners?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the prisoners who were in prison, it's their superior who decided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who issued the order for their detention. We were just a service who executed and kept the person who was imprisoned by whoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am confused completely now, because all these orders are addressed to the central military prison, but I really have no more time. Can I now see please P 01806 from the second bundle. It's a report from Mr. Stanko Bozic submitted to Mr. Coric and Mr. Marcinko. It's a report on the work of the prison for March 1993. I will read only one paragraph in Croatian. It's the last sentence on page 1. In English it's on page 2. That paragraph says: "In the course of the month, we received two visits from the ICRC, whose entry into the prison was approved by the chief, Mr. Valentin Coric." The report does not mention that the International Committee of the Red Cross had any comments or negative comments about the situation in prison. You can see it there. And I'll continue. I suppose that there were no complaints because otherwise they would be noted in the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. Could you indicate where you quoted from because I have the document number P 01806 in front of me, and I do not find the passage that you have quoted from page 2 of the English version. Oh, I'm sorry, I found it. I'm sorry. It's okay. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to call another document, P 02853, also from our second bundle. P 02853. It's a report for the month of May 1993, again from Mr. Stanko Bozic, addressed to Mr. Coric for May 1993. I will read out a couple of points that are interesting to me. First, the first two sentences, to follow up on what we discussed before, it says: "On the 9th of May, 1993, upon the outbreak of conflicts, for security reasons, we received 1.820 persons into our institution, who remained a couple of days." That is the first sentence. And then the last sentence on page 1, it continues on page 2. It says: "In the course of the month of May, we had regular visits from the Red Cross. Representatives of the ICRC notified us that they were satisfied with the correct conduct of employees, but we also received a complaint that isolation cells were inadequate and that we should not place a single prisoner inside them." Now, I read out to you the comments about May 1993, comments from the ICRC, and I don't see that there were any other complaints such as about mistreatment of prisoners. If there had been any, they would also have been in this report; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I need to correct the transcript my colleagues tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two small questions on this document. It transpires from this document that 1.820 displaced persons spent some time at Heliodrom. Do you agree with this figure? It's from your superior, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he wrote that correctly, because he got this indicator from the employees who worked with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of May, we saw that 518 were released. If we do the maths, I see that other people, some other people, stayed in Heliodrom. And on the 26th of May, 1993, we see that Mr. Pusic took eight persons for an exchange. From your recollection, did "refugees" stay or did they leave, or did maybe some new ones come after the 18th of May, because eight days later, on the 26th of May, we see that there was eight of them who needed to be exchanged. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since large numbers were coming in, and it's mentioned in this report, some immediate releases followed at various -- following various interventions and orders. As they were coming in, they were also leaving. As for these eight detainees that were taken over by Mr. Berislav Pusic, in the last passage it says, "for purposes of exchange," which means that those persons were in prison on that day and then they left to be exchanged for somebody else, probably members of the Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a quick question. In the next paragraph I see that Mr. Rade Maricic had escaped, but what's curious, it says a "detainee in the civilian prison." Does that mean that your military prison had also become a civilian prison? Because it's your own boss who says so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This detainee who was placed, according to what Mr. Bozic writes here, he was a detainee of the civilian prison, and the civilian prison was located in Ricinova Street in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how come then that Mr. Bozic, who is the chief of the military prison gets interested in somebody who is in a civilian prison? I rather have the impression that Mr. Rade Maricic had been transferred to your prison, the military prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been the police who caught him the same night he escaped, or maybe caught him later and put him in our prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would also like to ask a question. A few moments back we had a list of persons released which went up to the 18th of May. Some people were released on the 16th, 17th, and 18th of May. You remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In your -- in your diary, on the 15th of May, you write, "All those removed from the zone of war operations have been released." You must have been wrong in your diary. So it's not reliable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The diary is true. It's only my recollection that I cannot trust completely date -- to a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you then saying that the document shown to you by counsel, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, was false? Because there you have released -- lists of persons released or the 16th, the 17th, and the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this part, when a report is written it was written 19th June but covering the month of May 1993. And Mr. Bozic reported all events and developments for the whole month of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not taking this further. I'm not saying that I'm satisfied, but I don't want to take more of your time, Counsel. I'm sorry. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify once again, because there is a general confusion about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when they arrived, we referred to them as displaced person or refugees. At that point, at the same time, there are other persons to whom we refer as prisoners or detainees. They are separated, and they had been in the prison from before because they're either serving sentences or awaiting proceedings against them, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So throughout the time when the displaced persons were there and continuing in the month of May, policework continues. Some new prisoners arrive. They are processed by crime prevention and security officers, and they are placed in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when, in this document, we refer to exchange and detention, we are not talking about the people who were under Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda. We are talking about the people who were being dealt with by the crime police or SIS and who do not belong to the category of displaced persons. They belong to the category of prisoners who were separated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last thing from this document, that is the last two sentences: "The number of employed officers is 24. Deputy commander Pero Marijanovic is on sick leave as a result of being wounded in street fighting in Ricinova Street." Pero Marijanovic is mentioned here, who is on sick leave on the 19th of June because he was wounded in the fighting. Tell me, Pero Marijanovic was one of your guards, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that military policemen, including Pero Marijanovic, were also engaged on the front line in combat?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pero Marijanovic was wounded on Ricinova Street. I think he was wounded when the military investigations prison was being relocated from Ricinova Street to Heliodrom, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he was on sick leave?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, do you know whether military police was also engaged in combat on the front line? I'm not speaking only about your experience in the prison. You were a military policeman. Maybe you should know.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I never moved anywhere from Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this report we saw that the number of employed officers was 24. You told us the number of guards was around 16. If I understood correctly, apart from the guards, another three of you were employed: Mr. Bozic, Ms. Cvitanovic, and you. That means 3 plus 16 makes 19. Here we see 24. Will you agree with me that, in fact, the number of guards was not always the same, it varied?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now call on e-court from our second bundle P 03209. It's a document shown to you by the Prosecutor during his examination-in-chief. It's a report you wrote for Mr. Bozic concerning the incident with volleys of automatic fire. I will not read it. I will just ask you some questions. In the report it says the following: That the military police from the prison security informed the brigade police about the incident, and the deputy commander of the 3rd Brigade, and that after that an agreement was reached according to which the brigade military police was to conduct the processing. Now, I assume that the perpetrators of this incident were soldiers from units put up at Heliodrom and that it was the brigade military police that was in charge of them and not your security service, and that for that reason, it was the brigade military police and the command of the brigade was supposed to take measures linked to this incident. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, hypothetically, had your police security service for providing security for the prison, had they stood up to the perpetrators responsible for this incident, am I right in thinking that all that could have happened would be to fan the flames of the incident? The consequences would have been much worse had they done so; is that correct? Had the military police from the prison security physically stood up to the people doing the shooting, they just would have made the situation worse with more adverse consequences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they didn't allow them to enter. They didn't allow them anywhere near the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, counsel, this is a bit of speculation, "What would have happened if." MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll continue with the questions and then you'll understand why I'm asking this and why I think I have grounds to conclude that. And I think that my next question will clarify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until now we had determined the number of military policemen providing security for the prison. We have established which units were stationed at Heliodrom. We did this during the examination-in-chief. Now just tell me one more thing. Is it true and correct that according to the instructions for the work of the central military prison, dated the 22nd of September, 1992, which you're well acquainted with, a military policeman doing security detail within the prison building did not -- was not allowed to have either long-barrelled or short-barrelled weapons but all he had was a rubber truncheon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, because of what I've asked just now, I think my hypothesis was quite logical. It was quite logical and feasible. I'd now like to move on and discuss the 30th of June. When you previously spoke about the arrival of a large number of persons on the 30th of June, 1993, you said that when they were received and their names taken and criminally processed and that it was the crime prevention department and the SIS and the MUP that did the processing. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the 30th of June, 1993, did unauthorised persons bring in various orders in respect of these people and that they did not respect the orders given by the authorised personnel and thus made work in prison impossible, the normal work of the prison impossible? Do you remember incidents like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, may we have on e-court the following document -- we're going to show two documents -- or, rather, three documents, and then we'll discuss them. The first document is P 03193. It's in the second bundle. And it is a document signed by Mr. Zvonko Vidovic on the 5th of July. It is a special report. And I'm reading from paragraph four where it says the following: "According to the list approved earlier, 81 individuals from the category of the over 60s and under 18s have been released, but 16 juveniles were refused passage on the last check-point before Mostar, they were returned, although the list with the names of these individuals for whom this bus transport was organised was supplied to them earlier. The check-point commander, Tomislav Primorac, was informed about this omission made by his soldiers." May we now move on to the next document. It is document P 03238. Once again a special report by Mr. Vidovic dated the 6th of July, and I'm reading from paragraph two: "Seventy persons were released who had passed the military commission which established that these persons should continue treatment in a hospital. During the release of the last group of detained individuals, an incident occurred involving three young unknown soldiers from Siroki Brijeg, the Siroki Brijeg battalion, who forced out, from a bus, 30 individuals with valid medical clearances and at gunpoint returned them to the SVIZ premises. Following a similar incident which took place the previous day at the check-point to the entrance to Mostar, in my view, we should stop with this way of releasing persons until we are given orders that regulate the attitude of soldiers towards the detained individuals. I have to add that yesterday in the SVIZ a written order arrived signed by Colonel Obradovic emphasising that, without his signature, there can be no visits or release of detainees from the SVIZ Heliodrom." Now, tell me, were you aware of this incident? Do you remember that events like this took place and whether Mr. Vidovic, who signed the document, is the same Vidovic that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your answer yes to both parts of my question, because my question was in two parts?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes to -- well, there were problems. People were returned. I remember that very well. The persons as stated were returned from the check-points, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we now have a document from bundle 2. P 03201 is the number, and it is the order from Colonel Obradovic mentioned in the report of the 5th of July, 1993. All I'd ask you to do is to have a look at it and to say whether you are acquainted with the order, whether you've seen it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move on to the following document: P 03351. It is also from the second bundle, and it is a report from the defence department for the period of January and February. In Croatian, it is on page 6, and in English, on page 8, and I'd like to focus on point 2.4. This is something that the Prosecutor showed you earlier on. So I'd like to read it out again. Point 5.4, and I'm interested in the last paragraph. "The military police has the task of providing security -- the security of the prisoners. Forcible entry into the prison was noted, and forcible conducting of investigations by certain commanders. Conduct -- behaviour of this kind should be prohibited once and for all and rendered impossible." Tell me, please, do you know that unauthorised individuals, as it says in this document, for example, the commanders of various units, the soldiers of the units like those put up at Heliodrom, did forcibly enter the prison? Which means, despite the fact that the guards and you were opposed to this, they nonetheless entered the prison. Did you have knowledge of cases of that kind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in two instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the following document: P 03254 on e-court, please, in the second bundle as well. And it is an order from Mr. Stanko Bozic dated the 7th of July, 1993, in which it says the following: "The order by Mr. Valentin Coric to prohibit entry -- all unauthorised entry into the prison". Am I right in saying that from this order we can see that Mr. Bozic was aware of this kind of conduct and that with the help of Mr. Coric he attempted to prevent these incidents on the basis of this order?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you told us, and I'd like to go back to the crime processing, you said that the crime prevention department of the military police processed individuals brought in on the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before broaching that subject, I'd like to go back to a point. Based on the documents shown by the Coric Defence, it would appear that the military police under the authority of Mr. Coric recounted the situation, and it seems that P 3201 was about this, that Colonel Obradovic had authority to release prisoners, because he says, on the 5th of July, nobody was to be released without him having signed. So Mr. Obradovic was not a member of the military police. He was from the 1st Brigade of the HVO, Knez Domagoj Brigade. Now, how do you see the situation? Does it mean that as of the 5th of July it was the 1st Brigade that had tutorship over the prison, authority over the prison and authority over who was to be released or not? Was that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- the order from Mr. Obradovic, I remember it well. It was not complied with because he wrote the order and because Heliodrom, allegedly, was in the area of responsibility of the army he was in command of. And I remember after that that this order was conveyed to Stanko Bozic, and he was told that it was not meritorious and that we came under the authority -- we, the prison, came under the authority of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the crime prevention department of the military police who processed individuals brought in on the 30th of June, 1993. That's what you said. Now, tell me this: The processing includes interviews, interrogations, does it not, and it's standard policework, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next document, P 03651 on e-court, please. It's in the second bundle. And it is from Mr. Zvonko Vidovic. The subject is the decisions taken at a meeting held in Ljubuski on the 22nd of July, 1993, in the military police administration. The document is dated the 23rd of July. I'd like to read the document and then we'll discuss it. I'd like to start with paragraph two where it says the following: "The activities and competence of the crime prevention department were reiterated once more at the meeting. It was assessed that direct collaboration with the active-duty police, the military police and the MUP, and the District Military Court was good. The initiation of proceedings was wholly clear, and there was no overlap, while our cooperation with the officers of the central military investigation or remand prison must be indirect. A mediation is achieved through the District Military Court for which we process crimes to the extent of evaluating whether there are grounds for bringing criminal proceedings, and the SIS, inasmuch as cooperation is necessary. "So all the individuals who were detained, where criminal proceedings were not taken or criminal reports filed, as far as our department is concerned, it is under the -- on the order of the chief of the military police administration, unknown to our department. This refers solely to a large number of Muslims who were brought indiscriminately to the SVIZ, the central military investigation prison building, and then forgotten. Through inertia, the crime prevention department conducted interviews with over 2.000 people, but not a single one of them was of any interest from the aspects of crime prevention. The question posed of Mr. Valentin Coric, the chief of the military police administration regarding our duties was therefore justified and was the reason for him issuing the order for us to start dealing with crime. "After the head of the department of administration and justice had to compile a report on the SVIZ, that is to say the prison, pursuant to decisions of this department, it is the task of the warden of the SVIZ to name a department of justice -- that a department of justice should be appointed and that all decisions be taken by it. As concerns disciplinary measures against HVO soldiers, these will be decided by the person issuing them. We believe that there are a certain number of people who are of interest to security among the 2.000 brought in indiscriminately to the SVIZ. They should be found and processed, which is a job for the information and security service." Now I'd like to ask you the following: From this document, can we see that the chief, Valentin Coric, sent this -- a letter saying that their job was crime detection processing on the basis of which a criminal report can be filed as well as the fact that people who were not suspects and were not suspected of having committed crimes did not come under the authority of the crime prevention department of the military police. Have you understood what I've said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, may I have your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday my colleague Ms. Nozica showed you document P 04775. We can show it on e-court, but I'm sure we all remember the document. It was the proposal with the schematic for work in prison which you sent to Mr. Rado Lavric whom you considered at that moment to be the responsible person in the military police and who could help resolve the situation. Do you remember the document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I feel, when I read out the document from Mr. Coric a moment ago, where the department of justice and the crime prevention department of the military police is raised and their authority and power with respect to the SVIZ, that Mr. Coric explains the situation precisely in the way in which you did, that you proposed on the basis of your schematic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm moving on to another subject. Shall we take the break now, because I have a couple of documents which are quite long? If it's at all possible, could we take the break now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish. It's 25 past. We are going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now going to look at two documents from the second bundle. First, can we have P 03942. It's a report from Mr. Bozic from the 4th of August, 1993, addressed to Mr. Valentin Coric and Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic. You have already seen this report, so I will very briefly retell it because we have no time. It describes the situation at Heliodrom post-30th June, and it describes the problems you encountered starting with health problems, including lice, jaundice, and some other diseases among prisoners, unpleasantness with ATG Baja Kraljevic, and the problem of shortage of officers. In this report, in the last but one paragraph, it is mentioned that for a while you had eight home guards given to you for assistance. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was from the 4th of August. And now I would like to see P 04031 from the same bundle. It's a report from Mr. Branimir Tucak from the administration of the military police security service, dated 8th of August, 1993. That's four days after the previous one. And then Mr. Tucak relates again the occurrence of lice and scabies, the shortage of military policemen, and asks for reinforcements. Do you remember that Mr. Tucak was also in the control department, that he came to inspect?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met with him two times. He did come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we look at the date, we see that Mr. Tucak came to inspect two days after Mr. Bozic informed Mr. Coric of the situation at Heliodrom. We just note this from the documents. In your diary, in the entry for the 14th of August, six days after the date of the report by Mr. Tucak, I see that you wrote on Tuesday, seven new military policemen would come as reinforcements. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we look at the situation in which home guards were sent to you and attempts to send reinforcements, would you agree with me that after the requests addressed by Mr. Bozic to the extent of what was possible, there were attempts to send you reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Defence has referred to reinforcements, and you needed them. That's obvious. Still, in this last document, we see that you had 2.000 prisoners. You used to work in civilian prisons. In 1993, though, there were international treaties and documents, and there were standardised ratios between the number of prisoners and the number of supervising personnel. Were you aware of those standards or were you completely ignorant of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you -- are you aware that in 1993 Mostar town was divided into sectors for purposes of defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some divisions, but I can't remember them. I only remember the responsibilities of Mr. Mijo Jelic, because he was the one who maintained contacts, and I heard that he had been appointed for the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to clear that up through a couple of questions. Do you know that Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic, until the beginning of August 1993, apart from being commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the military police, was also commander of the central sector or the central zone of the Mostar defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in that period before August 1993, and I'm asking you this because it's evident from the Prosecution documents that you reviewed and said you reviewed, do you know that until August 1993 Mr. Mijo Jelic issued orders for prisoners to be taken out to work for the requirements of other units, too, such as ATG Mrmak, ATG Zrinko Skrobo, ATG Benko Penavic, 2nd Battalion of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mijo Jelic, after August 1993, was commander of the Mostar defence and in that capacity issued all orders related to the defence of Mostar including orders to take out prisoners for labour?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew he was commander of the town defence, and he had powers to have prisoners taken out to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that it was common practice at the prison, at the time when Mijo Jelic was commander of the town defence, that for the purposes of any unit that needed prisoners for labour, orders would come to Jelic and then down to commander of the prison, Bozic, and from him, down to the security commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to move to another subject. Could we call on e-court from the first -- sorry, from the second bundle. There are two documents that we will see. The first document of the two will be P 04902, an order from Stanko Bozic of the 9th September, 1993, where he says -- it's still not on e-court. P 04902. It's called "order", and it says: "It is strictly prohibited to take any prisoners out to work beginning with the 10th September, 1993, at 2000 hours." Next document, please. P 04927. It's a report by Mr. Stanko Bozic dated 10th September, 1993, which reads -- I'll just read the first paragraph: "On 9th September, 1993, I performed an inspection of the prison and observed, among other things, prisoners who had been injured and who wrote their own statements on the circumstances of their injuries, that I attach hereto." Now, am I right in concluding that Warden Bozic, in his inspection of the 9th of September, learned about cases of injuries to the prisoners and reacted by issuing this order prohibiting prisoners to be taken out to work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can we call on e-court P 05881. It was shown yesterday by my colleague Ms. Alaburic. It's an order from General Petkovic, dated 14th October, 1993, a month after Mr. Bozic's order prohibiting prisoners from being taken out to work in any of the brigades' zones of responsibilities. When we look at this order, we conclude that General Petkovic was trying to assist Mr. Bozic and had to issue this order, because the prison as such, headed by Mr. Bozic, did not wield enough authority to prevent occurrences of prisoners being taken out to labour with all the implicit violations.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now see P 06202. It's also from the second bundle. It was shown to you previously by the Prosecutor. It's a report by Mr. Stanko Bozic of the 28th October, 1993, addressed to General Petkovic. Mr. Bozic thereby informs General Petkovic that units are failing to comply with his order forbidding detainees to be taken out for labour, and I conclude that the units did not, after all, obey even the order of General Petkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now call on e-court P 06819. It's an order from Mr. Stanko Bozic of the 23rd November, 1993. It's an order that reads: "Order forbidding prisoners from being taken out to work, pursuant to the general order of General Milivoj Petkovic of the 14th October, 1993. This order enters into force again as of 23rd November, 1993, at 1500 hours." Just tell me, why does it say the order enters into force again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Bozic, again, contacted the competent superiors and wrote this order. He didn't write it just like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were the said units accepted -- exempted from this order?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all from the 3rd Brigade, and it was at the locality of Heliodrom barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It means because that whatever works they required, they would be performed within the perimeter of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that there were cases that units deployed at Heliodrom would take out prisoners on the pretext that they would be working within Heliodrom, and then without informing the prison authorities, they would take them outside?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that about -- I heard about that coming back from my sick leave. I heard that they were taken out to places where they sustained wounds, and some people were even killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another subject now. Can we call P 06848, both in English and in B/C/S. We'll look at the last sentence. Before that, I would just like to remind everybody that we have already discussed cases of unauthorised entry, forcible or violent interrogations, violation of orders prohibiting entry to Heliodrom. Now, this is something you saw before of the 24th November, 1993, a report that you sent to Major General Ante Roso, head of police Rade Lavric, chief of defence Jukic, and in the last sentence you say, on the 24th November, 1993: "It is my opinion that it is high time to take some steps to improve the work of the prison and to improve security, as well as to decide exactly who is authorised to take out prisoners from work or to order them to be taken out for work, that is, in whose jurisdiction the prison in Mostar is." I suppose this reflects the situation as it was in Heliodrom in November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says in November, whereas my question was up to November, throughout year 1993. Can we now call on e-court P 04756. In Croatian it's page 3. In English it's page 4. Fourth paragraph, I believe. It's in our first bundle. It's a record or minutes from the senior staff meeting of the department of defence of the 2nd of September, 1993, and I'm going to read the passage now. "Thereafter, Mr. Coric presented certain problems faced by the military police. Primarily due to the engagement of military police on the front line, quality has been lost in the personnel of the military police, materiel and equipment are being taken out by unauthorised individuals, and work is very poor in military prisons." And then the chief took the floor and said: "My opinion is that we have two military prisons, that is, Heliodrom and the military prison at Ljubuski. As for other places of detection, Gabela and Dretelj, I do not consider them as military facilities..." And so on and so forth. Tell me, please, do you know -- are you familiar with this situation regarding the military police? You agreed, it seems, that the situation was exactly as described by Mr. Coric at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know that the military police went out to fight on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know because you didn't know about anything that happened outside Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just repeat your answer. You said, "Yes, but I didn't know that the military police went out to the front line." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to something that you discussed with Ms. Nozica. Just a moment. Let me find it. In response to her questions, you said that, as the warden of the prison, you represented yourself as such and signed documents, and after the meeting with Mr. Franjo Cvitkovic at which you received his order to tighten the security service in prison. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your diary it is noted that the meeting took place on the 26th of August, 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now going to take a look at two documents briefly. They are documents P 05457 first, please, on e-court. The document is in the Prosecution bundle but not in ours, unfortunately. It is 13/3, part 3 of the third bundle. Otherwise, it's P 05457. And it's on page 2. It is titled "Instructions." We've already looked at this document. Ms. Nozica showed you it yesterday. But anyway, it's a set of instructions from you about the books to be kept for detainees taken out to perform labour. Now, on page 5 of 186, please, may we see the signature and the date. The signature says the 20th of August, 1993, and your signature as prison warden. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's something you've already looked at. Now, the next document on e-court, P 04367. Page 2 on e-court. It's also an instruction by you. And also at the bottom I would like to have a look at the date and the signature. It says the 20th of August, 1993, prison warden, and followed by your signature. And from this I can see that both these documents were signed and compiled six days before the meeting with Mr. Cvitkovic. That is evident from the documents, so I don't require an answer from you. Next document on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, counsel. Are these really two different documents or is it two times the same document, because it's the same date and the handwriting looks pretty much the same. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] It has been registered as two different documents by the Prosecutor, that's why I read them as such, because we have two e-court numbers. And they're actually different in content too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can assist. The reason that there are two different exhibits in the bundles is because they were put in the face -- they were put in the front of two different logbooks, one for the prison and one for the school and sports halls. So yes, there are two bundles that both have this document attached or glued in or stuck in the first few pages, but we can certainly ask the witness to tell us that it was the same document put in two different journals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Praljak, are these two documents that we have seen that are written by hand, is it two times the same which was simply copied and used in two different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This book was made for one building, and the other book was made for the other facility where the detainees were accommodated and given out to perform labour. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I asked for 4530, the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to have this question clarified. Can we have the two documents, the original documents, next to each other on the e-court? Is it not possible to have -- okay. Well, then, I leave this open. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] It is a Prosecution document, or both of them are from the Prosecution bundle. I tried to cover both. But my colleagues are now telling me that the point is that one document was compiled for one building and the other for the other building. So formally -- in formal terms, they can be treated as two documents. So perhaps in content they do correspond, but they were intended for two different facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am told by the registrar that it is possible to have them juxtaposed on the e-court and then we will immediately see whether they --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the hard copy of these documents and they can be placed on the ELMO. So if you wish to do that, we can try that as well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I just wanted to be of assistance, because even -- because when we put them side by side we'll see that they are the same except that the form of the documents is different and has two different numbers, because one was intended for one facility, the other for the other. We don't have time otherwise to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I take that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Let's move on to P 04530. P 04530.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the minutes from the meeting of the central investigating prison. The date is as we see it, 1993, 26th of August, and I'll read from page 1, point 2. There's a number 2, and it says: "Under the military police, which provides security for the prison, pursuant to a daily report to the warden." And I'll read another sentence from that same page, several lines lower down: "Logistics support to the prison should be provided by the military justice department." Let's see who has signed that. It says "Commander of the SVIZ," and then there's your signature, Witness, Josip Praljak. Do you remember this meeting and is this indeed your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer is yes. Right. Thank you. I just have a couple of questions to ask you. We'll be finished soon. Two documents, P 0 -- [no interpretation]. P 00514 is the number of the next document that I'd like to look at, please. They are instructions on the work of the SVIZ, the central military investigation prison in -- of the HVO in Mostar, the 22nd of September, 1992, and you said that it was in force throughout 1993. Now may we take a look at the first page after the title page. So page 1 after the title page, and look at point 1 titled "The duties of the warden of the central military prison of the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar." I'll read that out. Point 1 first, please. "The prison warden is responsible for the overall work and life in the prison. He is responsible -- he shall be responsible for --" I read the prison commander, not prison warden, to make a distinction there. So I read out the prison commander, not prison warden. Yes, prison commander, as it says on the document. So: "The prison commander shall be responsible for all the work and life in the prison. He shall be responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. He shall supervise the following every day: Security personnel, the building and rooms, prisoners of war, and military prisoners. "He shall take all necessary measures on the spot to remove all inadequacies observed with regard to the service. He shall assign security organs and all daily activities in the prison every day through a daily order." Then under 7: "He shall receive representatives of the Red Cross visiting the prison ..." And point 8: "He shall maintain direct contact with the MUP, the military court, and military prosecutor." And point 9: "He shall send in reports to the military police administration." Tell me, please, were you -- you've already told us that you were aware of the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'd like to move on to my final area. And may I have on e-court P 06844. It is a document shown to you yesterday by my colleague Ms. Nozica, and I'll just ask you something very briefly from that document. It is a report by Mr. Perica Grujic from the crime department of the military police linked to the conversation he had with you, and he reports that with the 24th of November, 1994 -- or, rather, the report is dated the 24th of November, 1993. I'm not going to read it. I'm just interested in certain details. I don't want to read through the whole report because we went through it in detail yesterday. Tell me, please, are you aware of the fact written in this document, according to the fact that ATG Baja Kraljevic had its own policemen? That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that a person mentioned in this document as Reuf Ajanovic was a person who introduced himself as Stjepan Barbaric and conducted certain investigations under that name?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another point: When you looked at these documents yesterday, you told Ms. Nozica that you didn't hand over the documentation as it says here in this document, but the warden Mr. Bozic. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have P 06626 on e-court now, please. It is in our first bundle. It is a report by Mr. Stanko Bozic sent to Mr. Branimir Tucak on the 12th of November, 1993, which is to say, 12 days prior to the conversation with you, mentioned in the previous report shown to you by Ms. Nozica, and it says: "Subject: Photocopying of SVIZ documentation. "On the 9th of November, 1993, on the basis of a written request number -- of the 8th of November from commander Mladen Naletilic aka Tuta, the documentation on the release of Muslim detainees between the 1st of July, 1993, and the 4th of November, 1993, was handed over for photocopying. "The photocopying was done by Captain Reuf Ajanovic in the presence of employees of the SVIZ, Mr. Josip Praljak and Mr. Zdenko Drljaca." Now, tell me, did you know about this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Bozic wrote it, I -- although I can't remember it now, I must have been present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were present, does that mean that you perhaps forgot, but that you were the one who handed over the documents and not Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the report, I don't think Mr. Bozic would have wrote a report contrary to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your answer to my question, yes, then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, I have two more questions. You told us that you had no contact with the women detainees.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.
