utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your diary under the 2nd of November, 1993, the entry there, you recorded that you handed over their letters to the SIS employee in the presence of Lutko Pehar. How can you explain that if you had no contact with the women?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter was seized by one of the guards. I can't remember who, and he brought the letter to our office, and I forwarded it to SIS, who was the authority over us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have an entry where you say that Lutko Pehar and to the SIS employee, you put to them all the problems that the prison was facing. Why did you do that rather than Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered that, as I was the fifth member of the commission, and as I took my appointment seriously, I thought that that was what I should do. And many other things that I did, I did by virtue of the fact that I was the fifth member of the commission in order to improve the conditions at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 11th of November, you were already working or considered that you were already functioning as the fifth member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered myself to be a member throughout, because the order never arrived to say that I had ceased to be a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have another short question. Tell me, please, do you remember that on the 31st of December, 1993, 23 files of the Heliodrom were handed over to Lutko Pehar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was president of the commission for storing the archives, and I think this process was completed in April 1994, pursuant to an order from the chief Zeljko Siljeg. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would conclude my cross-examination here, and I would just like to inquire if there is some time left, because my client would like to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much -- how many minutes do you need, Mr. Coric? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Not too many. Fifteen minutes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, wait. This could be a problem, because Mr. Ibrisimovic should have one hour, Mr. Karnavas -- what did you envisage, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in light of the questioning so far, I will not be needing the entire time. I have no objections at this time to give Mr. Coric some of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Proceed. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Cross-examination by the Accused Coric:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Praljak. My questions will be very specific and clear, and I would appreciate answers of the same kind. Did I ever call you at your office in Heliodrom by telephone? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I do remember that I did. I called you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recall that, but not many times. Five or six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, do you remember? In which period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was at the time when Mr. Bozic left to his other work. We talked to each other then. But if any other dates, maybe you can remind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when Mr. Bozic was away for a month or so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was February and March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- so you don't remember telephone calls from me. Do you remember if I called Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you invited to the senior staff meetings of the military police administration, Bozic or yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, but if Bozic went, I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll ask other witnesses. It's important to me to hear from you. Have you ever seen a document in which I ordered something to you or Mr. Bozic apart from that instruction of the 22nd September throughout my time until I left the military police? As the Prosecutor said yesterday, it was October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, to be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to be specific, because we heard yesterday some suggestions that I sent orders to release or not to release people, do you remember a single document from me on that score?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only document that I saw when I was reviewing, actually, I saw your name next to Berislav Pusic's interceding for the release of one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that I needed Berislav Pusic or another underling to get somebody released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take part in that. Maybe Stanko Bozic wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, let's move on. We saw from numerous documents that the issue of the status of the military investigations prison always remained outstanding. Did it drag on all the way until I left? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Praljak, that you received a salary, Mr. Bozic, Snjezana Cvitanovic, Zdenko Drmac, at the 5th Battalion of the military police, the 1st or the 2nd Company, 1st Platoon? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were attached to the 5th Battalion of the military police, professional contracts were signed at the police. At that time, Mr. Anicic did not allow me, Bozic, or Snjezana to sign that professional contract, and we had, as a result, only half of the salary of an ordinary guard, because, and he said so in so many words, he considered us as civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to remind you of, because I have document P 04099. It's a list of the 5th Battalion, 2nd Platoon, working on the security of the military police of Heliodrom, commander Smiljanic, deputy commander Kozul, and both you, Praljak, and Cvitanovic and the others are on that list. It was designed so that you had some kind of salary. You were placed on that list pending the resolution of the status of the military investigations prison by the competent people.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm done with that and I have just a few more brief questions. In your interview to the investigators of the OTP, you said at the end, when the investigator asked you, "Do you have anything in particular to add?", you said the following: "I was always in touch with Mr. Ivo Lucic, assistant minister of defence for security and the chief of SIS, and I gave him verbal and written reports." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Ivo Lucic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking if you remember what I just quoted or at least tried to.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. About these contacts and reports to the assistant for security, did you report to anybody else, Mr. Stojic, myself, or anyone about these contacts? Did you inform us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a verbal contact, not in writing. And as far as I remember, that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned something in writing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I'm sorry. I didn't write anything to Lucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen numerous documents, and you said in your testimony and in your cross-examination that at Heliodrom prisoners of war were interviewed by officers of the SIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversations with Mr. Lucic, did you discuss that issue?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you discuss, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him about the work of the prison and the situation in the prison, and after that conversation, the next day, I believe, he sent Lutko Pehar to inspect the prison and see what the situation was like as for the SIS itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I therefore conclude that, after your talks with Mr. Lucic, the documentation of the prison was removed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't conclude that either before we see the documents and look at the dates.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question to conclude. What was your relationship with warden Mr. Stanko Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for our relationship, it was excellent until the day when the war archives were handed over. If you want to hear more --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No need. I read the documentation. Do you remember when Stojic and I left the ministry, Mr. Marijan Biskic was appointed assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Biskic, as assistant minister, at the first stage, issued an order that you should all submit to him reports about the past work of the prison, including all aspects, treatment and work with prisoners, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really familiar with that. Maybe Stanko Bozic, if he received that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Stanko Bozic was then appointed company commander for the security of all prisons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what prisons you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the admissions centre for POWs.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what -- that's when it was established, including Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stanko Bozic got that appointment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get an appointment then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I got an appointment, but verbally, I was appointed, and officially I was deputy warden of that collection centre for POWs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any appointments during the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first one I got, apart from that instruction to tighten security from Cvitkovic. We talked already about the 5th Battalion and what kind of status I had there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get that in writing from Mr. Cvitkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, but I did talk to him about it. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you claim that you had an order in writing, a decision in writing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It seems that everybody's dealing with Mr. Pusic from all sides, and I have to point out now, when it's my turn, that Mr. Pusic was not a magician or David Copperfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my questions will be brief and clear, and if you give me the same kind of answers, we will deal with it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a number of documents. Not all of them will be used in the cross-examination, but may I ask that these documents be handed to the Chamber, and there is a copy for Mr. Praljak as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to start off from the end so that we put an end to this story about the commission that you have been questioned by the Prosecution, the Stojic Defence, and partly, the Coric Defence. You know which document I'm talking about. It's that order from August 1993. P 03395. You keep stressing, Mr. Praljak, that you were the fifth member of the commission. I know Mr. Pusic was supposed to be the chairman, and you were supposed to be the fifth member. What about the other members? Were they all equal or were you somehow ranked one, two, three, four?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Pusic, I didn't know any of those officials, and I thought of myself as fifth in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said to Mr. Scott, to the Stojic Defence, and to the Judges that you don't know about a single meeting of that commission, and you were never present if they met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge showed you your diary yesterday, P 00352, and you wrote, I believe on the 24th -- sorry, on the 4th of November, 1993 -- 24th of November, 1993, that the commission was not meeting. That was 24th November, 1993, three and a half months after Mr. Stojic's order; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed that in that period, on the 5th of August, in fact, you received the order a couple of days later, you never wrote to the person who was supposed to be the chairman of that commission, Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "commission," I think of it as a collective body that's supposed to meet and discuss something. You said a moment ago that except for Mr. Pusic, who was supposed to be the chairman, you didn't know anybody else, Jokic, Barbaric, or Musa.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Zeljko only once during the war, and I actually properly met him after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is this: If you don't know those people, you don't mention in your diary that you contacted the other members of the commission in any way from the day you received the order.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have contact with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary you say you received that order on the 11th of August, and that's not in dispute, but the same order was also received by Mr. Bozic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you say there that you spoke with Mr. Bozic about that order.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But when I read what's written in the diary on the 11th of August, 1993, you said -- in fact, you wrote that, together with Mr. Bozic, you would be working on it and reporting to the chief and the chairman of the commission. But you said a moment ago that you didn't actually write to the chairman of the commission at all, and your interpretation of the order, if I understood you correctly, was this: "We agreed that we would jointly remove any deficiencies in the work of officers at the prison in case we observed them."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So that's how you understood the order and the mandate it imposed on the commission and you as the fifth member?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there is perhaps a detention centre in Prozor, in Donji Vakuf, in Stolac, in Vares?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand that, as a member of the commission, you had full control over those detention centres?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read it, I realised the commission would cover all the prisons in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have any knowledge or any communication with those prisons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You, as a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your knowledge was limited with respect to Heliodrom, and you even said that your authorisation was very limited; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, whether I'm right or wrong, if you have limited authority in Heliodrom, then that authority absolutely does not exist vis-a-vis any other facilities, just Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It just applied to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You can confirm that you had no knowledge about what was going on in Vares, Prozor, Stolac, Gabela, Litina, the silo, et cetera and I assume you've never even heard of some of these places, the Unis factory, for example, where allegedly there was a detention centre in Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any of those. I wasn't familiar with any of these detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, the order was one that Mr. Bozic received as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Mr. Bozic address the commission or you as a member of the commission in any written form.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were together in the same place, in the same facility and prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether Bozic wrote any letters to any of the other members of the commission or whether he had any communication with them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the only communication he had with any member was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this brings us to the 24th of November, the date you mention, and an entry in your diary when you say, and I'll read it out and quote you, because you wrote the diary, then you know what you wrote: "In view of the fact that the commission with President Pusic never held a meeting -- or Mr. Pusic never held a meeting," and then all the people you informed in these responsible positions. Did you know, on the 24th of November, that Marijan Biskic had established a different commission a few days after that which was supposed to deal with the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have the document in front of you. Would you take a look at it now. It is P 06810, and there's another one 723, P 0723 as well. Have you found the document, or does the usher need to help you? P 06810 and P 07023. Have you found it, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: P 06810 -- or 80, for the record. And it says -- Colonel Biskic says: "On the basis of a working meeting, I send you the names of the employees of SIS and the military police who are going to become members of the commission to tour the prisoners of war accommodation site, et cetera." And then he says that there will be Lutko Pehar, the operative in SIS and Sretko Tomic, graduate of law. Mr. Praljak, you're not there, let me say that straight away, nor is Mr. Pusic. Now, you said you haven't heard about the commission. I assume you haven't heard about this document or haven't seen it before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the next document speaks about a report on the work of that commission. I don't think that is something that we need address. Somebody else might take up that subject, some other witnesses, to explain what happened to that commission. But let me tell you that on the 24th of November, when you say the commission "was not working and not holding meetings" a commission was in existence set up by Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just so the record is clear, we're talking now about a different commission. It has nothing to do with the Pusic commission. I mean, let's be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in your pre-trial motion, as a foundation document for Mr. Pusic's accountability, you mention this document, but I claim that it was just letter -- dead letter on paper. It was never consumed. It never came into existence. But I think that that is a matter for another discussion at some later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I would like to know that because I think that's an important point. Then the Chamber should be advised. If it's the Pusic position that the Pusic commission never came into existence, and never was implemented, I think that's important for everyone in courtroom to know. If I hear that, that's what I hear being said. If I'm wrong, I'd like -- it can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Counsel Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was stated, Mr. Scott, when Mr. Tomljanovich was here and gave testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But let me go back. When you received this order, you said that you talked to Mr. Pusic over the telephone about the work of that commission and that Mr. Pusic said, "We'll do the work."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you had no further contact with Mr. Pusic in respect to this commission, did you, nor do you mention this in your diary at all? I find no entry to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go back to another area, another subject. The 9th of May is the date, 1993, and P 02260 is the document. It is an Official Note compiled by Mr. Bozic - we've already looked at that - about the release of people who were at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to throw light on this document from another angle. Were those people supposed to be there in the first place, and did Mr. Pusic act quite correctly if this was noted in the Official Note when he says, "release those people, let them go home, back to their homes"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who arrived on the 9th of May were civilians, women and children, men, too, and the reason for their coming was well-known, why they were displaced and the -- according -- and Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda said that this was just a place where these displaced persons were taken in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is, if Mr. Pusic acted as is written down in the Official Note, was that the right decision when he said let the people go home? They have no place to be here.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only those people, but none of the other people either should have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And then you testified that the people left Heliodrom very quickly after that, these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And I refer to the decision -- adjudicated facts from other trials, 109 from the Naletilic trial and Martinovic where it was noted that these people left Heliodrom within a very short space of time. We heard a number of questions about the position of Mr. Pusic in the military police, the post he held. It's a little confusing, but in your diary, I find entries in which you write and mention the name of Dragan Barbaric; right? On the 7th of December, 1992, the 5th of February, the 17th of February, and then in March 1993, and Mr. Barbaric was the head of the department, was he not, for crime prevention; right? So he was the superior to Mr. Pusic; right? In that chain of command, in that division; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marcinko was his superior as well, who was the department head or whatever his title was.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Pusic was not your immediate superior. Your immediate superior was Mr. Bozic, and it was from him that you received orders, and he would tell you what you were supposed to do within the frameworks of your remit in the prison; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to return briefly to an area that you were questioned on about the performing of labour and taking out prisoners from Heliodrom to perform labour. Would you take a look at the next document, please, P 002921. I'd like us to clarify certain points from a formal aspect. The document is before you. If you cannot find it, I'll ask the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 002921 is the number of the document. You know this document. You said you don't know who wrote the note at the end, Puljic who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was either the commander or a staff member who was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't you, that's the main point. You didn't write, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When we look at the top, we see that the request is sent by Mr. Puljic to Mr. Bozic. Now, you explain the procedure, that it would be sent to Mr. Smiljanic and then further on. So the request is sent by Mr. Puljic to Mr. Bozic. And it says, "I need 20, 100 people for labour." And Mile Puljic was commander of the 2nd Battalion at the time, he was a highly ranked officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is my opinion, that in this chain of command, if when we're to look at it and compare it, Mr. Puljic was far above Mr. Pusic, was he not? Isn't that right? That's my opinion. You can agree or disagree or if you don't know, say so. Answer, please. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecutor referred to these documents in the binders, the orders. We have more than 50 or 60 of these orders where Mr. Puljic issues orders, but he doesn't need agreement or any permission to do so from Mr. Pusic, does he, because in my opinion, Mr. Pusic is ranked below Mr. Puljic, is he not? Now, take a look at the second document, P 2638. It is an order by Mr. Mijo Jelic. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into what Mijo Jelic could do or couldn't do in his powers, et cetera. I'm speaking as it stands here, Zlatan Mijo Jelic is issuing a written order here for the requirements of such-and-such a unit. He says he needs, I don't know how many detainees, to perform labour, et cetera. Now, the Prosecutor referred to this kind of order by Mr. Jelic, and there are over 200 written orders of this kind. I did not find a single order from Mr. Pusic except those notes, those brief notes written down in handwriting. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav Pusic, as far as I remember, and judging by the documents, I never saw a single written order from him except when he phoned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic showed you the set of instructions, and Judge Trechsel drew our attention to the instruction you wrote about keeping logbooks of the detainees. It was P 04367, and he says nobody can take any detainees out without a written request and permission. And that was the procedure that was respected when it came to Mr. Puljic and Mr. Jelic. And I have no objections or comments to make on that score. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you a few questions, and my learned colleague asked you the question. You saw the document when Mr. Pusic was appointed head of the office for the exchange of detainees. I don't know if you know the mandate of that office. Mr. Pusic, as the head of the department of the office, was supposed to collect information from all institutions which can be used within his remit, and that was the exchange of prisoners and other individuals. So either from the military police or the prison or international organisations or privately obtained information. So information and facts which would help him work within the frameworks of his terms of office. Do you know about that? Are you aware of that, that you -- he had to undertake this gathering of information about individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us how the procedure to release persons was put into practice, and you speak about that in the diary. First of all, there had to be permission granted from SIS, then from the crime prevention department, and finally Mr. Pusic had -- once he had received all those documents, would give authorisation and permission for people to leave the prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were an experienced worker, you worked in institutions like that before the war, so everybody entering the institution must have a piece of paper and leaving must have discharge papers allowing him to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as I understand the situation, it was like this: The permission given by Mr. Pusic, finally, is a piece of paper which takes note that on the basis of previous procedure the person was allowed to leave prison. If it was not an order, it was permission and authorisation following on from the procedure taken by SIS, the crime prevention department, et cetera, and the office for the exchanges; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Scott showed you one such document as representative example, P 04686. If you could look at it again. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just try now. It's the same person. We have a document 6D 00169, which is a certificate from the crime prevention department, signed by Zvonko Vidovic, and he notes there are no criminal proceedings under way, and the certificate is issued for purposes of release of Zijo Droco from Heliodrom. And we have 6D 00168, a certificate from SIS Mostar saying that there is no problem with releasing Zijo Droco from Heliodrom. It's just as you said before. Everybody would give their approvals first and then Mr. Pusic. It's the same person, isn't he? These documents were also representative, as Mr. Scott called them. We have lots of such documents, and we will use the same procedure to tender them. A moment ago, when I asked you whether it was the right procedure, the SIS, the military police department, and then Mr. Pusic, you gave an answer, but it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, was the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed this in private session yesterday, so could we move back into private session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary -- in fact, you mentioned Mladen Jurisic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, he was military prosecutor, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same thing I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your diary that at a certain point you were informed that releases from Heliodrom are allowed only with the approval of the military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you just one more document. Maybe I didn't understand it very well yesterday in the transcript. It's document P 06436. It's the list of detainees of the SRZ of Mostar who have a letter of guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, SVZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I understood yesterday, but maybe I'm mistaken, when you answered the Prosecutor that Mr. Jerko Radic brought those letters of guarantee. But when we look at this, we see that Mr. Bozic informs the office of Mr. Pusic about lists of detainees who have letters of guarantees. That is quite the opposite. I asked you a question a moment ago about the mandate of Mr. Bozic. Am I right, Mr. Bozic is informing Mr. Pusic, not the other way around?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bozic informs who has letters of guarantees, and I said that Mr. Radic was down there most often. So he could have brought it to the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Just two more questions. Reading your diary that reflects the situation at the time, I think you probably recorded everything that was of any significance in that period and following your communication with Mr. Pusic, verbal and written, I don't think you had too many contacts with Mr. Pusic in that period.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Following all this and your testimony and the documents shown to you, I could say that you are probably not the right person to talk about him. There are other people who can say more.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed him, and I communicated him and had the knowledge that I had addressed him in keeping with what I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: These are questions, Mr. Praljak, which I have suppressed during the interrogatory by Counsel Tomasegovic Tomic, and they concern -- there are actually three. The first one, very simple. In your diary, it has been brought forward. You say, "We will get seven more guards on Tuesday." I did not find any entry as to whether they actually did come. Do you remember whether you actually got these additional guards? It's -- you noted that on the 14th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't remember, but there are daily reports that could confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then with regard to document P 04927, that is a document dated 10th of September where -- it contains a report about wounded prisoners, and I just want you to confirm that these were prisoners who had been wounded not by the ABiH but by HVO people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't possibly know who wounded any of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In that report, it is said that is inappropriate for a Croatian soldier to do something like that. You do not remember that report? It was shown to you an hour ago. Okay. I will not insist. The last question: We have seen that there were different orders saying that no prisoners must be given out for work, particularly in the front line and similar engagement, and you have said that these orders, particularly also the one by -- issued by Mr. Petkovic, were not complied with. Now, I do not quite understand. It seems to me that the person responsible for the prisoners, and this has been recalled to you what the duties of the prisoners were, according to another instruction, were to be in charge of the prison, full stop. Now, how, if there is an order of Mr. Petkovic, how come that, nevertheless, prisoners are handed out when this or the other unit, an entity far below Mr. Petkovic, asks for it? Why does the prison management not enforce the order given by General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time the order was received from Mr. -- General Petkovic, I was not at the prison because I was on sick leave. When I came back from that sick leave I saw that order. And as I explain to you earlier, I heard from other people at Heliodrom that generals -- the general's order was not being obeyed and that on the basis of approvals from Milivoj Petkovic, people can work within the perimeter of Heliodrom. And those same people who came and told me so were taken outside Heliodrom where there were cases of escape, wounds, and even deaths. And I wrote that in my report, mentioning also the understanding reached between Stanko Bozic and Stanko Sopta Baja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who is the most concerned here wants to say something. Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Can I have P 06848 in e-court, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we please call P 06848. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] The document is in e-court in the Croatian version. I don't know if you have the English version. I would like to ask the witness to find in this report a passage that begins with the words "Exemptions in the release of prisoners for work --" Have you found it? It's in the middle. It's the third paragraph from below. Mr. Praljak, do you see where it says: "An exception in the release of prisoners for work"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the 15th of October. General Petkovic's order came prohibiting prisoners from being taken out to work. Warden Stanko Bozic complied and even verbally demanded that prisoners be returned. Some were not returned even then. That's written there, isn't it? Let's go on. "An exception in the release of prisoners for work was made by the warden with the approval of the commander of the 3rd Brigade, Mr. Stank Baja Sopta for the needs of the same brigade and with the explanation that the prisoners would be working within the barracks on the following jobs: Logistics, kitchen, workshop, cleaning in buildings, cleaning of the perimeter and similar." Now, can I ask you this: Was it I, subsequently, or was it the warden himself who decided to make an exception to my order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I wrote this, the warden arrogated that right to himself and did that. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I read here. We have another document where the warden also seems to arrogated that right to himself. And the warden, in that document, allows logistics, kitchen and laundry service, et cetera. So it's not my order. It's his order. It's an implementation of what you will wrote in this report. Can we then conclude that the warden was the first to violate my order because he was the one who made the exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all the orders shown later, allowing the 3rd Brigade to take prisoners for labour, are exceptions. To explain, the 3rd Brigade provided support to the prison. They performed various household chores, laundry, kitchen, et cetera, and I understand that the warden was trying to make some arrangements that worked. And there was even a film showing 10 prisoners working in the kitchen. The Prosecution didn't show us that film. All those were logistical needs, that work that was also necessary for the prisoners themselves. Is it true what I said, that prisoners worked in the kitchen cooking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Did they work at the workshop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Did they clean the perimeter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to continue. You have interrupted me. You have been allowed to do so, but I think this is not interesting any more for the purpose I want to follow. Mr. Karnavas has quite rightly pointed out that you have not answered my question. And by the way, the order Mr. Petkovic has referred to, is one day before the 24th, namely the 23rd of November, and it's document P 06819, but we do not need it on there. But in this document, it also says that the order of General Milivoj Petkovic of 14 October becomes effective again on 23rd November. This is together with your own report very astonishing, because it gives the impression that simply that this order had not been complied with, and I wonder whether you had spoken with Mr. Bozic about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order of the general, General Milivoj Petkovic, was of such a nature, in one of its points, that only he and the Main Staff were authorised to issue approvals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, he's not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor soon. But please, Witness, General Petkovic said that, as of such-and-such a date, nobody should be working outside the prison. It was clear. So nevertheless, there is a document from your superior, Mr. Bozic, indicating that works are allowed after all, but in the kitchen, inside the prison, et cetera. But you who were specialised in the prison system, because you worked in it before the war, do you believe that in a normally functioning prison prisoners should work inside the perimeter on work such as carpentry, plumbing, kitchen, et cetera, and sometimes even outside cleaning alleys, reinforcing walls, et cetera? And finally, was Mr. Bozic order within the framework of the prison something normal? Let him answer and then you will ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to say that my client's order was not correctly interpreted. My client did not have authorisations, nor was the contents of his order such that it prohibited anyone from working outside the perimeter. My client, Mr. Petkovic, issued the order of the brigades of the operation zones to make certain requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please answer this question, whether a prison warden was entitled to tell prisoners, "You are going to work inside the prison to support the day-to-day life of the prison itself"? So at the time, at Heliodrom, is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Bozic, since there was -- since the meals were prepared in the kitchen and for cleaning purposes, people to work in the kitchen, to clean the main building, the area around the buildings, he would give permission to do that throughout. That was usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that between you and Mr. Petkovic there isn't any divergence. Do both of you agree in saying that despite the orders those people who were taken outside to do work, whether up at the front line or somewhere else, was done by units which came to ask for prisoners violating General Petkovic's order but profiting from taking advantage of the order issued by your warden, Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I understood. Now, it's 20 to 1.00. We're going to take a break for 20 minutes and reconvene, and then Mr. Karnavas will have time to ask -- to say what he wanted to say -- or, rather, for the cross-examination as well. He will have 30 minutes, and Mr. Scott will have 30 minutes, which will take us up to quarter to 2.00. So we reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. As you might recall, at some point I tried to intervene a little bit prior to the break, because I felt that the witness had not quite answered Judge Trechsel's question and that -- and I believe if I understood Judge Trechsel, he was trying to pin the witness down into acknowledging that ultimately the responsibility laid with the warden, the deputy warden or commander, or whatever his titles were at times, in ensuring that orders were complied with as opposed to passing the buck as it were and trying to blame everybody else other than themselves. I trust that the Judges are satisfied and therefore I won't go into that. Otherwise, I presume Judge Trechsel would have asked a follow-up question. Having said that, Your Honour, I don't believe there is any need to cross-examine this gentleman any further. We'd like to thank him for coming here to give his evidence, though, not without expressing our rather disapproval that he's been less than forthcoming in many of his answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will be objecting vigorously if it goes beyond the scope of the cross-examination, just to make sure that -- and it should be limited to 15 minutes, I believe, not half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, additional questions and redirect is always linked to the cross-examination, of course, so please stick to questions which relate to the cross-examination on the areas discussed by the Defence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak. Sir, as you know by now, our time is limited and I will be most grateful if you will cooperate with me and the Chamber to try to answer our questions in the remaining time we have as efficiently as possible. I would like the witness -- if the witness could first be shown, please, Exhibit 5D 02016. And if it's quickest, I have a hard copy that can be shown to the witness. It's probably the fastest way to proceed. And, usher, I may need -- in order to move as quickly as possible, I made need your assistance afterwards, please. If you could put that in front of the witness. Sir, you were asked on cross-examination by the Coric Defence -- you were shown this document, and the -- about the releases that were made in connection with this document, and I would just like to quickly show you a series of other documents, please, and this is -- well, with that document in front of you, if you look at number 1, the person listed at number 1 -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to intervene. At no point did I say that it was the release of prisoners putting them at liberty, nor does it say on this document. It is a list of persons who are leaving. That's all it says, who are leaving, and that is what I would like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll take it at that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the first name listed there and you'll see that -- Can I also, please, ask the usher if you could please put on the ELMO -- show the witness the original language version of Exhibit P 02386. If we can have that in e-court, please, because otherwise I don't have an extra English copy, I'm afraid. Actually, if you can take that and put it on the ELMO. Sir, if you have the B/C/S document 2386 in front of you, which the English language version is now on the ELMO, can you just confirm that the people listed number 1 -- now referring back to Exhibit 5D 02016, that the person listed as number 1, number 2, number 4, number 5, number 6, number 7, number 8, number 9, number 10, number 11, number 12, number 14 - if there are more I won't go into them - those are the people listed on the document that's now in front of you. If I can see the top of it for a moment, usher. P 02386. And if we can go -- these were all people that were released again on the authorisation, as the document says, with the approval of Berko Pusic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once again, sir, as you testified in the last several days, is that consistent with the procedure as you understood it, that no one could be released, at least in this circumstance, without the approval of Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this part is concerned, the 30th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Ibrisimovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I would like to object. If you look at the document of the 14th of May, 1993, that's the date. When we spoke about procedure, we spoke about the 5th of July when Mr. Pusic was the head of the office. Now, I didn't refer to Mr. Pusic in discussing these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, but other people did, Your Honour, and -- the Coric Defence did and the Coric Defence used the document 5D 02061. And the impression that was created, one way or another, is that these were instances of people being released that had nothing to do -- in which Mr. Pusic had nothing to do. And the Prosecution has documents showing that, in the case of virtually every person listed in 5D 02016, virtually every one of them were released on the authorisation of Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I did use P -- D2 -- well, the document, but I didn't say a single word in my cross-examination referring to Mr. Berislav Pusic in document 5D 02061 or his position or role linked to the document. The document was presented as a document of the office for displaced persons and refugees and it has nothing to do with Mr. Pusic, the document that I showed nor did I comment on in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the -- these documents were tendered and used for the purpose of giving the impression that the military police was not involved in the release of these people, that it was all being done by, what I'll quickly call, the department of displaced persons. All the documentation shows that, in every instance, everyone on that list was released on the authorisation of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to clear that up. Witness, there's a document here which seems to be an official document because it comes from your director, although I see on the B/C/S version that we have his name but without a signature. So it's from your boss. Now, having said that, this document has a stamp and all the rest, mentions Mr. Pusic, and it seems that he is approving the fact that persons 1 to 19 had been placed at liberty or whatever. Now, as far as you were concerned at the time, Mr. Pusic was named president of the office before. What was he doing on the 14th of May, Mr. Pusic, to your knowledge? On the 14th of May, what post did he occupy? What was he doing then? In what capacity was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Berislav Pusic, at the time, was an employee of the military police. He worked for the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I help out, Mr. President? I think you're looking at the wrong document up on the screen. The Coric Defence didn't show this document. It was Mr. Scott that's showing you this document, the one you have. But when we look on e-court, it's quite a different document. It's the document of the office for refugees and displaced persons. It's quite a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document on the ELMO is not the same as the document on e-court, Your Honour. That's absolutely correct. The document that the Defence used, the Coric Defence used, is 5D 02016, which is a list of people released, a bundle of documents about people released and no one ever said -- no one suggested that there was a contrary document. The document that I, the Prosecution, have now put on the ELMO is the document that I submitted for the purposes of showing that this list of people, all coming from this document, were all released with the authorisation of Mr. Pusic. And I have several other documents that show that virtually everyone on this list -- so if I'm not going to be allowed to do my redirect examination, I can just argue the points and make the offer of proof, but I have the documents in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Are we talking about 02016 or 02061 because we've got both numbers on the transcript. If we can just clear that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I have is 2016.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you Witness -- usher to -- this is exhibit now -- exhibit P 02393. And, again, if you'll show the witness the B/C/S version and please put the ... Sorry. This document by Mr. Bozic, can you again confirm that these people - if we have the time we could go through the list - that these eight people were being released according to this document ordered by Mr. Berko Pusic to release? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to do the other two documents, Your Honour. We'll tender them after because we don't have time to go through them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there are eight names here, four of which have the same name, Kajtaz, the same surname. Were these people civilians, military men? Were they people condemned by the HVO or what? We see the names, but I don't know who these people actually were. They could be Serbs. They could be detainees, persons convicted of something. So who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were people who were brought in on the 9th of May. They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the feeling that they're names, are they? Olga is a female name. Emina. They seem to be women. But you can confirm that based on the first names of these people; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are the names of women and relates to all those who were detained and mostly on the 9th of May, 1993. It was women and children who were brought in to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you recall or can you recall from seeing the list, which is P 02386, that, in fact, the Muslim women just mentioned by the President are all -- were all family members of the 3rd Battalion of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The question that was asked was whether these eight women were members -- family members of Muslim HVO soldiers? Were they related to the Muslim HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, where these eight names are listed, -- well, not in the document of the eight names, but in the document where there are 19 names, 19 detainees, there it is stressed that these were families -- family members of members of the 3rd Battalion. The list with the 19 names on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, looking at that document and based on the direct and cross-examination of the past several days, do you recall that that was one of the bases by which people that were brought in on the 9th and 10th of May could be released, is that if they were Muslim family members of HVO soldiers? Sir, if you don't know -- our time is very limited, so if you don't know, just say so. I will move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to ask one or two questions on this subject. Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, as long as it doesn't come out of my half hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quickly then, Mr. Coric, because normally at this point it would be the Prosecutor's turn, but in order to assist the Trial Chamber. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Was there a criminal investigation of these persons on this list, these women? They were 90 per cent women. Do you know about that as the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric -- THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were displaced persons, Mr. Valentin. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] What I'm asking you is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go slower. Go ahead and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who were brought in on the 9th of May, no criminal investigation was conducted. These were refugees. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] How is this then related to the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I link this document because it was authorised by Mr. Berislav Pusic for release, and he worked in the military police, Mr. Valentin Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Did you see a document today, dated April, on the status of Berislav Pusic in the criminal investigation department of the military police? Did you see it or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what he carried out, Mr. Valentin. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Did you ever hear that Mr. Berislav Pusic was a member of the commission for exchange of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the middle of July. He was appointed in the middle of July. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] That's another matter. But I'm asking you before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Is it possible that from that position Mr. Pusic, in the name of some exchange commission, did his job, did his work? I'm asking you specifically, the release after the 9th of May. Is it possible that Mr. Pusic, having left the crime department of the military police, was linked to the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if he was attached to the Exchange Commission but he was linked to the releases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could please show on this very point -- could you please show Exhibit P 01773 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of what Mr. Coric has just said, sir, do you see that this document dated the 1st of July, 1993, Mr. Zvonko Vidovic refers to the officer for control in the military police, Mr. Berislav Pusic, on the 1 July, 1993? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] This is a document, the date of which is the 1st of April, not the 1st of July, and it doesn't mention Mr. Berislav Pusic as an officer for control. But if you read the passage that I read out it said, either the office of the control or some other function but it doesn't say that he was appointed to any of these two posts. So, I repeat, the date is the 1st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now that -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] And he's not on the list any more in the staffing establishment, in the department -- crime prevention department as of the 1st of April, 1993, and that's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what is the date on the document that I've just put in front of you, P 01773? What's the date, sir, please? Is it 1st of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of July, the 1st of the 7th month, 1993. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I don't know which document you're looking at, because on e-court we have P 01773 and it says the 1st of April there. In the English version it says the 1st of April and you have both versions on the screen. So please read the document on the monitor on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then it's -- if that's the case, Your Honour, then I've been given the wrong number and I apologise. The document that I have been given is the one that -- is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we're looking for that, let's go forward on some other things. We'll come back to that. Sir, is it correct that you told us and some questions were asked to you about the treatment of prisoners and some of the things that were put to you, can you tell the Judges how often did you actually, you yourself, actually go into the space where the prisoners were held, either in the prison building or in the school or in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely, not often, because it was overcrowded. So it wasn't easy to visit, to make a tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know -- let me ask, did you know anything about -- anything that was going on inside of those buildings unless it was recorded by Mr. Smiljanic or one of the guards at the -- for instance, at the morning meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was reported at the morning meeting -- if I learnt about something at those morning meetings, then I would inform the superiors thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct then, sir, and can the Judges understand that, unless something that had happened since 4.00 the previous day, unless that was reported by Mr. Smiljanic, you wouldn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you raise that with Mr. Bozic on a number of occasions and Mr. Smiljanic the necessity that all information be reported so that you and Mr. Bozic would in fact know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The chain of command under -- at Heliodrom, when you were acting as deputy warden, did Mr. -- except when you were acting as warden, that is, when you were acting in the place of Mr. Bozic when he was away or unavailable, did Mr. Smiljanic ever direct -- report to you? Was he subordinate to you as deputy warden, or subordinate only to Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every order would go to the commander -- the warden. Beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Judges, if you can, in terms of the questions that were raised about the -- the condition and use of the isolation cells, again, during this time period, during roughly let's say May to November 1993, how many times were you actually in the area of the isolation cells, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I think the witness already answered that question when Judge Trechsel asked him. I think the witness answered the question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that he already answered this question, so what do you want to show with this redirect? He said that he went once or twice, which might appear surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's the reason I was following up, but if the Chamber is satisfied with that, then I'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He could be asked what prevented him from going more often given his responsibilities. I mean, that may be an appropriate question that wasn't asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Mr. Karnavas would like to ask that question or perhaps we can ask Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak why they never went to the Heliodrom and find out what was going there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going ask the question. Sir, at the time, you were a professional working in the prison system, and everybody who knows how the prison system works, knows that the administration -- administrative staff circulate round the prison. You said that only very rarely did you go to see the cells which might appear surprising to anybody who knows how the prisons worked, but then again, why not? What were the reasons, as counsel has suggested, that prevented you from going more frequently? Because in fact you didn't go to visit those cells. So why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went rarely only when one of the guards asked us to go, and I visited because the supervision over the solitary confinement cells and the prisoners themselves was performed by the SIS and crime prevention service, and there might be people there whom I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we know that in February and March you were the deputy warden. We know that. Now, secondly, we know that you were the number two man in the prison, and when one has a responsibility like that, then one should go and make checks and control the situation in the prison. So the functioning of a cell requires -- makes it incumbent on the administrative staff to supervise and control the situation there, and you said you didn't go. So what is the reason? Why didn't you? That's what we're trying to understand. Why did you not go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To visit the solitary confinement cells, when I say I went rarely, visiting the prison building and premises was done by the warden or the commander. So there was no need for me to go every day if my superior did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying, as far as the solitary confinement cells are concerned, it was the warden who would visit. So there was no need for you to go because he went. Well, we'll take note of what you said. We'll record that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: One would then assume that when the commander Mr. Bozic was not there, you would go every day. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because Mr. Stanko Bozic, during his time there, except in March, wasn't on sick leave for a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I think the question that begs to be answered is why yesterday, under oath, the gentleman said only twice, and now he's giving the impression, again under oath, that he went every day. Either he lied yesterday or he's lying today. In other words, he's committing perjury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We may examine this question, but let me add another question. Did prisoners -- did you talk to prisoners who came to you? Could prisoners complain and talk to you, or did you hear prisoners? Did you ask that prisoners tell you how things actually are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every prisoner who announced himself to the shift leader or the prison commander was able to come and talk to me and Bozic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no. I interrupt you. I do not want to know what prisoners could do. I want to know to how many prisoners did you actually talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a number, but there's a logbook in archives logging every interview, every conversation that was held in the presence of two witnesses. Among the witnesses would be the guard who brought the detainee, myself, and Mr. Bozic. If Mr. Bozic was absent, then it would be Mr. Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this courtroom there are a few of us who have quite a bit of experience with regard to prisons, so you shouldn't be telling us stories. If you work in a prison as warden or deputy warden, it's your job to walk around, to go in to cells, to see how prisoners are faring, to control the guards, and to check how everything is working, because if the warden doesn't do that, that could end in a tragedy. You said that you were number two, and one wonders what did you do there? You already told us you worked 8.00 to 4.00, but what did you do during the day? Did you spend the day doing crossword puzzles in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my workday, it was exactly as the commander proposed it to me. As for tours of the prison, I'm telling you again, there was no need for it, if the warden went around and spoke to prisoners. It was not necessary for me to do the same, because he would share his impressions and findings at meetings, and he wrote reports about them. I think I was clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, in connection with Mr. Bozic, did you find unfortunately that Mr. Bozic was part of the problem in terms of making sure that the right things were done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This goes beyond his direct examination and beyond the cross. This could have been brought up -- in fact, earlier today on cross-examination, the gentleman indicated that up until the time of the archiving issue that he had -- that he enjoyed a very good relationship. But nonetheless, I think this goes way beyond and again what the Prosecutor's trying to do now is to get the witness to shift, once again, the blame on somebody else. But this could have been brought out on direct examination. If they want to establish that this gentleman, with all his numerous titles, all the times that he signed as either commander or deputy or warden or whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you should do what you just did a moment ago. You asked the witness, "In your cross-examination you said this and that. Now I'm showing you a document." Now you have to tell him like you did before at what point in the cross-examination he made a certain statement so that you can ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, you just -- you yourself and the Judges just raised questions about the involvement of Mr. Stojic and Mr. Praljak in looking -- in going into the prison, asked about that, the relationship and whether they did their jobs or not. And my question, in fact, flows directly from that, but it's -- it seems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's a follow-up on the questions posed by the Judges, go ahead please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me, if I may. I'm sorry to interrupt, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I mean it's obvious -- excuse me, Your Honour. It's obvious that no one in the courtroom including, with all respect, Your Honours, are going to allow me to conduct a redirect examination. I've was given time, ever since it started, the Defence have been on their feet at every possible second. The Judges have used most of my time, so really it's a waste of time with respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Your Honour, but there's a very important point here. There is rule that any counsel, Prosecution or Defence, has to have a good faith basis for putting a question in any form of examination. If Mr. Scott's saying he has a good faith basis for saying that Mr. Bozic was the cause of problems in the prison, this raises another subject of enormous latitude. What I'm going to suggest, in the light of what we've heard from this witness and the questioning, that the Judges, at this point, put some questions to this witness about the -- about whether he knows of the reason why he was not indicted following his interview as a suspect in 2004, whether there was any understanding in that regard with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- Mr. Murphy has just made my point. There is no way -- there is no way in the next eight minutes that we're going to -- this is going to be productive. Now we're talking about it by asking the witness why he hasn't been indicted and this is just simply -- the Prosecution has provided -- been provided no opportunity to conduct a redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes are left. Go ahead, Mr. Scott, with some points that deserve clarification in your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the visit of the ICRC in May of 1993 and the suggestion that there were no complaints by the ICRC.
